And General Tolimir has spent a fair amount of time on the regulations and the duties and responsibilities of the security branch, and I would like to go into that to clarify some of those responsibilities and to try to highlight some of those responsibilities so you get a complete picture. And in that regard, I would like to start with 65 ter 1978. It has been MFI'd as P01112. And if -- for simplicity, I would like to be able to give the general -- it's a three-page document, and he would have a better time reviewing it if he, I think, had the three pages and didn't have to squint at the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, take your time. I believe, since this is dated - you can see it - from the Main Staff, 24 October, I recall that you came to the Main Staff in September, so this would have been a document created at the time you were chief of operations; is that right? But, please, take some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and for General Tolimir, while the general is reading that, we can go to the last page of both documents to see who has written this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this document, it was from the year 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that it's from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can't see the second page of this document, so if we could be shown that page. We don't have the document, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before I get to it: General, you have testified, and as have others, that the VRS adopted many, or the basic, rules of the JNA, and, in fact, as you've acknowledged in your cross, the rules regarding security and command were from the JNA. Especially, you spent a lot of time with the rules for the corps. Were there various times where the VRS had to adopt those rules to meet their own specific needs and circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've understood the question perfectly. We took over the rules and regulations governing all sectors from the JNA; the application of rules of engagement, the application of instructions, and so on and so forth. Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and you've testified to that. And my question was: At times, as the war wore on, did the Main Staff and the VRS have to adapt those older JNA rules or clarify them for the specific situations that it was facing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Experience, from practice, showed that there were weaknesses at all levels and in all areas so that it was necessary to issue instructions to subordinate commands in line with the rules and regulations taken over from the JNA. Many people were insufficiently trained for military service, such as reservists, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm sure you remember from the last trial, was there actually one part of the rules in the corps JNA regulations relating to who was the deputy commander of operations that was actually very much against what the Main Staff actually ended up adopting? I think you'll remember how you explained that in the last trial.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean a comparison with the remit of the corps command, a comparison with the organisation of the work of the Main Staff, then this was about the remit of the Chief of Staff and had to do with the following: The chief of the Department for Operations and Training was the person to stand in for him, and that is the difference. General Miletic, as chief of the Operations and Training Administration, did not have that remit because in the corps staff the organ for security is directly subordinate to the Chief of Staff, and the organ for mobilisation and manning is directly subordinated. At the Main Staff, there was a direct line between the commander and the Sector for Personnel Affairs. There was also an intelligence organ to which security was attached. That was subordinate to the chief of the sector, and the chief of the sector to the commander of the Main Staff. That may be what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Without getting into the details: As I recall it, you testified that the corps rules anticipated that the chief of operations became the Chief of Staff in the absence of the Chief of Staff, but the Main Staff did not adhere to that corps rule and it had a different rule that you've already described. Is that basically correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about the following: For example, the chief of the Staff Sector, he was also the deputy commander of Main Staff. In the case of General Miletic, as chief of the administration, according to establishment, he was not simultaneously a deputy staff commander; whereas I, who was General Miletic's subordinate, was chief of the Operations Department and at the same time deputy chief of the Operations and Training Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. And my only point, though, is that the -- if we look at the corps regulations, the Main Staff practice was different than laid out in the corps regulations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what respect. I only mentioned the part relating to the structure, namely that the assistant for Intelligence Affairs was subordinate to the chief of the Operations Department in the corps, and to him, the subordinate to him was the Mobilisation and Manning Administration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the latter part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you because we don't receive interpretation at the moment. The last sentence which was recorded ended with the words: "... and to him, the subordinate to him was the Mobilisation and Manning Administration." And then the interpretation and recording stopped. Could you please repeat what you have said after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a nutshell, in the corps staff there is an organ for mobilisation and manning and there is an intelligence organ, and at the Main Staff, that is not part of the Staff Sector. These are two separate sectors there. These two sectors are subordinate to the commander, the Sector for Mobilisation and Personnel; whereas the Sector for Intelligence is an administration as part of the Intelligence and Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, my only point is: Because you have testified, and we all agree, that the JNA rules formed the basis of the VRS rules, is it fair to say that it cannot be applied 100 per cent of the time because there are basic differences sometimes, as you've just described, so we have to be careful when looking at the corps rules? We have to be careful because it's not 100 per cent. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this rule about the remit within a corps, the only difference is the part that refers to the command of the Main Staff. This part was not identical, but the rules were fully applicable to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, had we followed the corps rules, under the corps rules, in the absence of Milovanovic, the chief of operations, General Miletic would have been the Chief of Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct because these things are not identical. His establishment position did not read also "deputy." And he did have a higher rank than most others. But until June 1995 he was equal to many others, and many in the combat arms organ were actually higher in rank than him -- he. But his establishment position did not have this tag "also deputy," as it did for me, or for somebody else who was at the same time a deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. We're saying the same thing. The Main Staff rules, in that case, were different than the corps rules were, and it had major significance for General Miletic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference at the command level. We are talking about the regulations about competencies in the corps command, and now you're drawing a parallel with the competencies in the Main Staff command. And those are two different command levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's my point. We can't use the corps rules to be 100 per cent applicable to the Main Staff because there are differences; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part where the rules were not applicable, they were, indeed, not applied. It is my impression that the rule on competencies appears, because it was drafted. However, the rules on competencies had not been drawn for the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my question, and thank you. Now, as you've had a chance to look at this document, you were back from your injury for a few weeks when this document was drafted, does this -- does this familiar at all to you, this document about -- entitled "Instructions on Command and Control Over the Security and Intelligence Organs of the VRS"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've not seen this document before. It was not addressed to any of the sectors. It was drafted in the Main Staff. It was recorded under a number which I don't know. It was probably registered with the Administration for Security and Intelligence or the Sector for Security. I don't know where exactly. It was signed by the commander. Maybe I can read a "za," "on behalf of," here, but the typed signatures of the command of the Main Staff. In any case, it was intended for the subordinated units, i.e., corps commands, to the air force and the Centre of Military School, although there's not a clear list of addressees. However, I assume, looking at the contents of the document, that it was intended for the subordinated commands --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you have -- before I got off track a little bit. You did say at times the Main Staff had to remind the VRS and educate them regarding the rules, something to that effect, in place, and so I want to go over these instructions, as I believe they're very similar to the instructions -- or the rule that General Tolimir went over, to see if there are any differences or not, in your view. And I don't know if you remember, but the corps rules the general went over were dated 1990, the time of the JNA. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that's correct. However, I believe that he also quoted some of the things from the rules of service of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you -- that's correct. And would have those been from the JNA years as well? Do you remember the years?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used those rules from the former JNA, regardless of the year when they were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm just trying to get an idea of how much older those rules are than this 1994 rule. Do you remember the year of the security rules? Or if you don't, that's fine, we'll be able to -- I note that we were able to go back and look at that document, and it was 1984. Does that sound familiar or would that be within the range you would expect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We used those rules because after 1984, there was new -- there was no new edition in the JNA. If there had been a newer edition, we would have used that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just go over some of these to help get your views on them, given that -- would these be an updated version of those older rules, in your view?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This instruction was based on those rules. It was drafted as a result of certain things that appeared in practice and in the work of the subordinated security organs and subordinated commands. This instruction was intended for subordinated commanders. I'm judging that from the contents thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we were to be looking at the rules and procedures documents from 1995, these particular instructions would be a better or a more updated view of the underlying rules; is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the author of the instruction based things and initiated things that he had in focus. He wanted to highlight some things in order to improve the work of the security organs and the commands in which those security organs operated. Under item 1, the author draws everybody's attention to the focus within the remit of the work of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about that. It says: "The field work of the VRS security and intelligence organs primarily includes intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks which, depending on the situation, make up about 80 per cent of their total engagement. The remaining 20 per cent of their engagement consists of administrative and staff, military police and criminal-legal tasks and duties." Now, we didn't see that percentage in the rules that General Tolimir went over, but is this your recollection of how it was divided up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the rules of service for the security organs, there are no percentages; there are just activities. However, the author of the instructions directs people towards a certain focus, how much time they should spend on one activity, how much on the other, and how much on the third. The author of the instructions broke the work down into percentages to help them perform their duties properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would this be an example of the VRS adapting those JNA rules to its own specific circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These tasks are also contained in the rules. However, the author just wanted to break the work down and express the work and the portions of that work in percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you very briefly, if you can -- we see that it's -- there's two kinds of work: the 80 per cent work and the 20 per cent work. The 80 per cent worked is called "intelligence and counter-intelligence." And can you just, in the simplest terms, tell us what intelligence is and what counter-intelligence is? But very simple. We don't -- we've heard a lot about that already, but I just want to be able to distinguish it between the next, the 20 per cent tasks.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence work is aimed at collecting intelligence, at analysing that intelligence, and presenting that intelligence to the superior command. The intelligence refers to the enemy deployed in the zone of combat activities, its intentions, the situation -- or the overall situation in the zone of intelligence responsibility of the subordinated unit. Counter-intelligence deals with preventing enemy intelligence activities targeting one's own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us one example of counter-intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be detecting and monitoring the enemy intelligence organs, their intentions, as well as any individuals engaged in such an activity targeting one's own unit. The way and methodology of detection differ from one service to another. I would not wish to go into that, because I was never a member of any intelligence organ. In any case, they use all sorts of means, and this can be listening in telephone conversations, intercepting radio communications, electronic surveillance. And when something is detected or discovered, measures are put in place to prevent and discontinue any further activities of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Detecting security threats or traitors from within one's own ranks, where does that fall in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of the remit of the security organs. That's how they detect those engaged in illegal activities aimed against one's own unit, amongst their own ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that fit into counter-intelligence or intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That was very clear and helpful. Thank you, General. Now, the second part, the 20 per cent, mentions: "... administrative and staff, military police and criminal-legal tasks and duties." General Tolimir spent a fair amount of time on what appeared to be military-police-related, so can you just give us the same nice, concise -- your understanding of what military police and criminal-legal tasks and duties would be?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military policing referred to those tasks that are carried out by the military police. This most commonly implies providing security for command posts, facilities of special importance, providing security for a commander who is either stationed or on the move. In one segment, this also deals with the regulation of and control of traffic. So those would be tasks under the military policing remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what was meant by "administrative and staff"? That's the first thing that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the command level. The higher the level, the more pronounced the needs will be for administrative and staff duties. They are relative to planning, manning, replenishing the equipment and the assets level required for the unit of that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "unit," what kind of unit would the security officer be involved in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to military police units and their staffing and manning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, lastly, "criminal-legal tasks and duties"? Again, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the tasks would be to make arrests of perpetrators of crime within one's unit. Also, collecting and securing evidence to prove the crime in question. Also, submitting such evidence to legal bodies for further proceedings. When I say "legal bodies," I mean investigative bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've seen, in this case, military police guarding and interviewing prisoners of war. Would that be part of their duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I failed to mention just a while ago. In military police companies, at certain levels, there were crime departments, and that was their remit. They were the ones that carried out interviews as needed. Members of those departments belonged to the military police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And my question about prisoners of war. We've seen military police guarding and sometimes questioning prisoners of war. Would that be a part of their duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, that was done by members of the crime departments on the strength of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. That's very clear. Can we now look at the paragraph 2: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form a part ..." So if that was a brigade, they would be commanded by the brigade commander. If it was a corps unit, it would be the corps commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you recall hearing this important concept repeated in the JNA corps rules that General Tolimir read; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in this case, this is the same as what the corps rules had already said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on and says: "... but with regard to professional activities, they are controlled," or "managed," in English, probably, "controlled or managed centrally by the security and intelligence organ of the superior command." So I want you to be able to explain that a little bit. But, first of all, does that mean that, for example, the security officer in the Zvornik Brigade would be managed and controlled by the security officer of the Drina Corps, along this professional line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the rules that is quoted in here, a reference is made to the command of those units and who has authority over that command. And then later on it says that in professional terms it is the intelligence and security organs of the superior command which are authorised to command it. So when we are talking about the brigade, then their superior professional body is a body in the corps. We have already discussed that when we discussed the term "control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would it be true that the corps security branch would be professionally managed by the Main Staff security branch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the professional tasks such as planning, training, manning, materiel support, and similar tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic is the chief of security of the Drina Corps, he would be professionally managed by who in the Main Staff? Who would be his first-line professional manager in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the administration which is within the intelligence/security sector of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the chief of the administration, Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've already told us who Beara's direct supervisor is. All right. Can you -- again, this idea of professional management, can you give us an example of what that would involve? For example, can Colonel Beara issue a directive, tell Popovic to do something?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That level is not busy with writing the directives. He could instruct and talk about the training of the security organs, about the training of the military police, about manning. He can instruct as to how to perform the professional aspect of the task. That's why we say that he is being managed by the superior command and, more precisely, by the professional, specialised organ within the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when, for example, Popovic receives an instruction from Beara, does that have the effect of an order if it's in the proper course of his professional duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order is something that should be viewed separately. We are not talking about issuing orders here. Commanding is within the authority of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of an administration may not issue a task to the military police battalion within the Drina Corps. This is within the authority of the commander. However, through the security organ, in the professional aspect, he can help general, professional, and specialised training in order to enable the military police to perform their tasks in a professional way. But when we are talking about assigning tasks, that is something done by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does the commander many times decide the task of the military police by receiving proposals from the security officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. You mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. He was the security organ of the Drina Corps. The exclusive authority to command from item 2 rests with the commander. The chief of the Security Administration helps him in planning, organisation, and professional carrying out of the police tasks, which are to be carried out by the unit within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand that, and I agree with you. My question, though, is: When, for example, Popovic makes a proposal to Krstic, his commander, on how to use the military police, will his commander then issue an order, if he so chooses, based on that proposal?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already explained in my previous testimony what a proposal means, not just the proposal by the security organ, but generally speaking, so I can merely propose to the commander to use a military police unit. Whether he is going to adopt my proposal in its entirety, or partially, or whether he's going to amend it, that depends on him. And whatever he adopts, he is going to order. Regardless of whether it was adopted in its entirety or partially, he is going to issue it as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if General Krstic, in this situation, adopts the order -- adopts the proposal of Popovic or decides to do something else that he wants to do, can he pass that order down to the military police through Popovic? Or does he have to go find the military police commander himself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order will go directly to the military police commander in the form of a memo or a document. Normally, it is an order issued to the unit on the level of, say, a battalion. And the operative man is going to write out this order, the one who belongs to the operative organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I understand that the commander issues orders to his subordinate commander, and I agree with that. But my question is: Can Krstic, in this case, pass on the order through the security officer as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a written document. But if it's not, then he is going to simply pick up a phone and issue an oral order. If it's a written document, then it will have to be drafted in the staff, it will have to be logged within the operative organ, and then forwarded to the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, it's a very simple question. Can General Krstic, in this context, pass on an order to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic that Popovic passes on to the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can, but that is going to be the commander's order. Whether it is going to be written or oral or whether it is going to be Colonel Popovic who is going to carry it to someplace, that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But if you're the commander of the military police unit in the Drina Corps and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic comes to you and tells you to get in some vehicles and go to a mountaintop, you're going to follow that instruction, aren't you? That passing on the order through Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic has the thrust of an order but from, of course, the commander, passed on through Popovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I know that the commander issued that order, I'm going to carry it out. If not, I'm going to try to find a way to verify; for instance, if I don't like something in that order and I feel that I should verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since the witness already answered, I don't want to pose another question. I only wanted to say that the question should be clear and unambiguous. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Colonel Beara issued an order or passed on an order, a very serious order of some sort - say he was in a brigade area like the Zvornik Brigade - and he passed it on to, say, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, would that commander be able to go and speak to General Tolimir or someone else of authority at the Main Staff to determine the validity of that order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in this case one level was skipped, and that's the corps command, the Zvornik Brigade commander should verify whether that is actually the task to be performed. If he received this written order, then he should report to the corps commander and tell him what kind of task he was assigned. So it means that, yes, he is supposed to carry out the order, but he should also inform his immediate superior about that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So the commander of the brigade should go up to check on the order to the -- his corps commander. That would be General Krstic. If General Krstic had the same concern about the validity of the order, who should he contact?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should verify the authenticity of that order with the commander who has the power to command him. That is the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if the commander of the Main Staff was in Belgrade and unavailable and the order had been passed on by Beara, who should the Drina Corps commander contact?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, if the commander is absent, he is going to designate one of his assistants to deputize for him while he's absent, and that person deputizing for him may not command unless those orders are in the spirit of the previous decisions and orders issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's the next section here we've already talked about, but: "With regard to professional activities, they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organ of the superior command." And then: "This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations, based on the authority set forth in the law and the authority of the appropriate superior organs of the service, and applying methods and means of work in accordance with law." So, General, now here it says that the security person is under the command of the commander, but then it says, in regard to intel and counter-intelligent work, that there is full independence. Do you understand what General Mladic is getting at? How can you be under the command of the commander and yet have full independence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This independence is limited to the realisation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks. This means that he doesn't grant him a general autonomy, but only limited to this kind of tasks, intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks. This autonomy does not carry with it issuing orders, but only professional directing in carrying out of the tasks belonging to those two areas of work, intelligence and counter-intelligence. I think that this is not in contradiction with the rule that we quoted earlier, the rule about the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Would -- the professional supervision by the security officer of the military police in their handling of prisoners of war, would that in any way be considered an intelligence or counter-intelligence task or does that more fit in with the military police legal task side of the thing we've heard about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking care of the war prisoners is, according to the rules of the former JNA, something falling within the purview of the logistical support. And as we said that a moment ago, people from the Crime Technical Department can carry out informative interviews and, that is to say, gather intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Logistics officers guard prisoners of war? How many logistics officers are there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, we are now talking about officers here. Those people have to be accommodated somewhere. They have to be given food. And that is within the competence of the logistical support. Other people from other areas will take on the work from their purview, for instance, the Department of the Morale, Religious, and Legal Affairs, and then those inspectors, or I don't know how to call them, people who are supposed to carry out informative interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let me give you an example of a specific incident we have in this case. You've already spoken of the military police battalion that was attached -- or, excuse me, the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment which was part of the Main Staff. Now, if the soldiers and command of the 65th Protection Regiment military police unit were guarding hundreds of Muslim prisoners and they were being professionally supervised in that task and organised by Ljubisa Beara, would that task that Beara was involved in, organising these prisoners and their holding, would that be -- well, where would that fit in? Would it be the 80 per cent in counter-intel, or would it be the other part, or would it be something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was not a part of the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination. Furthermore, the Prosecutor here speculates about who organised the guards. This witness cannot know that. He was not in the Main Staff when this was going on. He was not on the spot when this was going on. So his answer can only be a speculation. I would like this question to be reformulated so that it is clear to the witness and also so that it is in the line with the situation in which the witness found himself at the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you'll recall the general having this witness discuss specifically the work of the military police, the supervision of the military police work by the security branch, and with the old rules. We now have this clarification before us, and all I'm doing is taking an example, based on these rules, to get an idea of if this is part of the supervision as outlined in the rules that the general brought up. He's brought up the rules. He's defined how they are. He's left a lot of gaps on what things may mean for this case. And I would like for you to fully understand the most recent rules on this point and how they apply, in particular, to this case and this example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would agree with you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, it's a simple question. If the MP battalions and their command is guarding hundreds of prisoners and Colonel Beara is there providing organisation, would this fit into the intel/counter-intel, the military police aspect, or something outside of what is anticipated by the rules?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules do not mention percentages. This is mentioned in the instruction. And the number of 80 per cent pertains to the intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks. Physical support, guarding of the prisoners, is not something that falls within the purview of these two activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, in this -- there's evidence in this case that military police are guarding prisoners in Bratunac, hundreds of prisoners, that they're guarding hundreds of prisoners in Zvornik, and their security officers are overseeing these tasks. Don't military police get involved in guarding prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't deny anything. I merely said that this task, guarding the war prisoners, is something that doesn't fall under either intelligence or counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does it fall under the military police work, as we see in the rules? The security organ oversees the military police work. Is this sort of military police work, looking after prison ers, something that a security officer would be involved in, or could be involved in, according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speculate about that now. If a military police unit was available at a certain moment, if it wasn't engaged in combat, then maybe the commander could have made a decision to engage it in providing the security. He can do that, and he can do that for any unit that was available nearby and that wasn't engaged in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, it's a simple question. The military police are guarding prisoners. Would it be in the remit of the security officer to professionally supervise them in that duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this task is not either intelligence or counter-intelligence task. The rules say that he controls and manages the professional aspect of the work of the subordinate organs of security and military police units, and this is not a task from that area. And the rules say that it is those tasks that he is managing, professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to invite you to answer the question. The question was not in relation to intelligence or counter-intelligence. The question was: "Would it be in the remit of the security officer to professionally supervise them," that means the military police guarding prisoners, "in that duty?" Could you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the rules do not define guarding as the professional task of the security organ. Whether they were able to do that, the security organs of the Drina Corps or the Main Staff or of some of the brigades, well, I don't exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No one is suggesting a security officer is actually guarding prisoners. The question is: The military police are guarding prisoners; would the security officer -- would it be in his remit to professionally supervise or organise or assist in the military police's job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't understand you so that it would be security organs who would do that. I'm talking here about the engagement of a military police unit who, at a certain moment, is guarding people who were captured. And then I say this is not within the remit of the tasks defined by the rules, in part, when they talk about the professional management or control of the military police units by the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if Colonel Beara was assisting the commander of the 65th -- the military police unit of the 65th, if he was supervising his work in the collection, detention, and guarding of hundreds of prisoners, he would be working outside his remit by the rules?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That work that was done is outside of the scope of work of counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not the question. Please focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can be, but it is not professional assistance or professional supervision, as the rules say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think everyone is very tired. I know I am. I have -- this is a critically important area. We're not through with this document. I have documents by General Tolimir that I believe are examples of these very principles so that we can see how they work in the field and get this witness's view on them. I have evidence, more material, related to chemical weapons. I have more material related to the directives, the issues that were brought up. Directives are key. Issues related to security command. I now have an issue related to the professional supervision of security officers and the military police. I've got evidence related to the treatment of war prisoners at the Rogatica Prison, which the witness said -- talked about. I've got issues related to the Muslims crossing over the Drina, which the general brought up with this witness. Basically, I would like it if this witness would come back so that I can finish my work. And if the general has more questions - I know he does - I have no objection to him finishing up his work. I hate to do that, to bring a witness back, I really do, and -- but this witness needs -- well, I better be careful. This is, you know, the witness's situation. But I'm sure we can make any good arrangements to bring him back. That would be my request, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you get the floor, Mr. Tolimir, I would put one question to the witness. We have a document on the screen. The subject is "Instructions." You'll see that just below the date of the 24th of October, 1994. Can you just please read into the record what is the subject of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour: "Instruction on Command and Control Over the Security and Intelligence Organs of the VRS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was my only question for you. Mr. Tolimir, you've heard what Mr. McCloskey told us. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Neither in the direct examination or in the cross-examination was this matter raised. Secondly, what Mr. McCloskey asked questions about was outside the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, whereas he was asking questions about the Drina Corps. Thirdly, this witness is not an expert for legal matters. He only speaks about provisions of the rules that he knows. He said that this was not the proper work of these professional organs. Whose proper work it is, is for the Trial Chamber to decide. If I need the witness anymore, I can call him as a Defence witness. I wanted to do a favour to both Mr. McCloskey and the witness and reduce my cross-examination to less than three hours. I don't mind being convicted for what Mr. McCloskey was speaking about - that's also for the Trial Chamber to decide - but I put it to you that the witness is not the one who should answer these questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In order to make one point very clear again,

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was your decision to shorten your cross-examination, only your personal decision. Several times you were told you have six hours and even more for your cross-examination. You didn't use that, this time. And you may continue, as Mr. McCloskey indicated, when the witness will be called back. We should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you in a position to provide us with some more information about your estimated length of your re-examination, about the topics you want to raise - you gave us some indication for that - and the reference to that part of the cross-examination you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And could we let the witness go, and I can go into that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to have a clear record now and to be able either conclude today or to recall the witness, but we need some more information, if you are able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On page 7, there was a discussion about hand-grenades that render the enemy incapable, and there was lots of talk about chemical weapons and gas. I have evidence that there was more than just hand-grenades and rocket-propelled chemicals. I have documents like the one we saw before, with -- and an intercept that indicates there's more than that. And given that this witness first said there were no chemical weapons and then said that they never used them and then spoke with General Tolimir for a long time about their use, I would like to bring us back to reality and show some more evidence of chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't need more information about the specific topic. Now we know the topic, the issue you want to raise, and you gave a reference. Could you do that in relation to other parts of your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. On page 24, lines 1 through 25, there was a question about Muslims crossing the Drina and their ability to cross the Drina as if it was no problem. This witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough for -- Judge Nyambe wants to put a question to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, I just want some clarification. As I understand your submission, reflecting from page 118 - that's what my transcript is saying; I don't know what everybody else's is saying - from on page 118, lines -- starting from line 7, you have said: "Mr. President, I think everyone is very tired. I know I am." I agree with you. "I have -- this ... critically important area. We are not through with this document. I have documents by General Tolimir ..." And you go on and you go on. My question is: The questions you seek to ask, in the context of your submission, did this arise in your evidence-in-chief and the accused person's cross-examination? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Judge Nyambe. And I was thinking of that as I was sitting down. The -- as you'll recall, this witness is the chief of operations. And while I had him outline, roughly, the Main Staff, we stuck to pretty much the detail of the chief of operations. I didn't ask him anything in depth at all about the important intelligence and security branch, General Tolimir's job, and the various rules. He identified Beara and Salapura, and that was it. I did not get into that at all, the rules, nothing. And, of course, as the chief of intel and security, these rules, the relationships between command and the military police, are fundamental to this case. Fundamental. And the general went through those rules, both the rules related to the security branch and the specific rules related to the military police, and how the security branch supervises them, and he went into it in detail and a very long time. And so he went right in to the heart, in my view, of this case, right into the heart of his responsibilities that you need to understand. They're difficult. I keep hearing them over and over again, and I need to hear it over and over again. That's the guts of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just need you to concede that the issues you want to talk about further were not covered in evidence-in-chief or cross-examination. We will find another way -- maybe what you need is to find another way to deal with those issues. But my understanding, unless I'm very wrong, the issues that are referred to do not appear to have been raised in your evidence-in-chief - maybe they have been raised yesterday when I was not present - or certainly not in the accused's cross-examination today. That's my understanding of your question that you raised. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In all do respect, Your Honour, I didn't -- you're correct that I didn't bring up anything to do with the intel and security branch. I didn't, aside from the basics. It was General Tolimir that brought it up. He brought it up for a long time, and he talked about the specific rules. He talked about the old JNA rules from 1980, from 1990. This thing we've talked about is the -- like he said, they need to remind people of what the rules are. This is a crucially important and clarification of those rules. They're the very things that General Tolimir was talking about; the same things, the same wording, the professional supervision, the commander in charge of the -- the commander and the command of the security officer. We're talking about the same thing. It's directly what he talked about. And if you remember, he referred to General Obradovic as an expert in these areas, and I agree with him. General Obradovic is a trained officer, he's a general, and he -- most -- many times he's able to provide a very clear explanation. The explanation he gave of security and of intelligence and counter-intelligence and ... was perfect, and that was brought up by the general. Those terms were used in his discussion but left in the open air. When he brings up items, throws them out there, doesn't fully cover them, calls a witness an expert, I would like to be allowed to ask this expert to tell us, When the general went over counter-intelligence and intelligence with you, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey and all other participants, we have to stop now because the tapes are running out. We don't have any time left. Just for a short moment, I would like to consider the situation with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can't sit longer today. The Chamber wants to postpone a decision about your request. We can't do that today. We have to check the transcript, the cross-examination, the issues you want to raise. We will do that at a later stage. For today, we have just to adjourn. The witness should go home to take part in the very sad celebrations. He has the right to do. And we will let him know if he will be recalled or not. That is not decided today. We come to that at a later stage, and we may continue our discussion about this procedural matter next week in the courtroom, and everybody should be prepared on that. And both the parties and the Chamber will review the transcript. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Thank you, Mr. President. And I, of course, would like to be able to respond to all Judge Nyambe's questions, and look forward to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all have the time to prepare a continuation of this discussion next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In this case, I have to remind you, sir, until you're finally released from your duties as a witness, you have not the permission to contact either party about the content of your examination and your evidence. But the Chamber will let you know when this will happen. Thank you very much. We adjourn and resume on Monday, 2.15, in this courtroom.
